#7801. I Thought Multi-Tools Were a Gimmick — Then I Took One on a Camping Trip

If, like me, you think multi-tools are gimmicky gadgets, you might change your mind once you discover how handy they are when your toolbox isn’t within reach.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

I admit I scoffed when my partner first started raving about his Leatherman Wave+ multi-tool. I thought it looked like an expensive, over-elaborate gadget that was destined to gather dust in a junk drawer.

However, as a keen hiker and camper, I’ve discovered how useful it is to have pliers, knives, a saw, scissors, files and other tools packed into one compact, quality piece of kit. I’ve also watched my tech-obsessed partner regularly reach for its precision tools when tinkering with his electrical equipment.

Ahead, I’ll share how a tool I once dismissed as a gimmick earned a permanent spot in my pack, and what two experts think makes a Leatherman worth the price tag.

I had to realize that our Leatherman Wave+ isn’t meant to replace a well-stocked toolbox to understand its value. Instead, it fills the gap when dedicated tools aren’t conveniently available or really needed.

At home, I regularly use the tool’s tiny scissors to carefully prune dead leaves from our many houseplants, the knife to open packages and the small screwdriver to tighten the legs on my glasses. My partner is an IT professional who also has an impressive collection of synthesizers, and he regularly reaches for the tool to make small technical repairs and splice wires.

I’ve found the Wave+ even more useful when we’re borrowing my parents’ campervan, hiking, or camping. The bottle opener is handy for those after-adventure beers, the serrated knife slices baguettes for trailside sandwiches, the saw cuts small, dry branches for kindling, and the screwdriver has adjusted our portable stove and tightened folding chairs.

The pocket-sized multi-tool packs 18 functions into a stainless-steel form that measures just four inches when closed and weighs 8.5 ounces. Alongside the tools I’ve mentioned, it has pliers, bit drivers, a wire stripper and crimper, a ruler, an extra knife blade and file, and an admittedly slightly-tricky-to-use can opener.

While I don’t regularly use all 18 tools, and I might never use some, having the selection provides peace of mind, especially in remote places.

Daniel Kilburn, founder of Emergency Action Planning and a preparedness expert, has carried his Leatherman Surge since his military service in 2006. “It’s an expedient tool to have on hand when you know you’re going to be someplace where you won’t have access to any others,” he says.

Scott Emanuel of knives, multi-tools, and outdoor equipment retailer Heinnie Haynes is also a multi-tool convert. He appreciated having one for quick fixes while renovating his cottage, and particularly rates the needle-nose pliers, which rival standard models rather than acting as an emergency substitute.

Kilburn suggests multi-tools can be a useful starting point for someone who doesn’t own a toolbox, and at the other end of the spectrum are the tinkerers and prepared problem-solvers Emanuel sees as natural fits.

“The person who will value a Leatherman is the one who spends their after-hours in the garage building stuff that they probably never need, it’s the kind of self-reliant and prepared person who you rely on to solve a problem,” Emanuel says.

The Leatherman Wave+ currently costs $129.95, meaning it should be a well-considered purchase rather than an impulse buy.

It’s reassuring to know that you’ll be investing in a refined product designed because of a genuine practical need. Founder Tim Leatherman conceived a pliers-based multi-tool after encountering car and plumbing problems while traveling through Europe in the 1970s, and after careful development, he launched the original Pocket Survival Tool in 1983.

Today you’re paying for that established reputation and durable construction, and Leatherman backs its products with a 25-year warranty.

“They’re ridiculously well built, really well regarded, and their choice of tools is good,” Emanuel says. He describes sought-after Leathermans as the “collectible top end of the multi-tool market.”

Kilburn recalls seeing lower-priced multi-tools failing his comrades during their military career. “Some disintegrate over time because they were just cheaply made with poor-quality material [and] poor-quality steel,” he says. His Leatherman Surge, meanwhile, has lasted over 20 years. If replacing it again, he says he would choose Leatherman over his backup Gerber multi-tool because he prefers its feel and durability.

Leatherman makes a wide range of multi-tools, so it pays to consider which functions you’ll genuinely use. The Signal model adds outdoor-focused features suited to camping, including a ferrocerium rod, emergency whistle and sharpener, but omits scissors. I use scissors enough for plant pruning, first aid and gear repairs that the Wave+ remains the better fit for me.

If you’re unlikely to use most of its functions, a smaller, cheaper multi-tool could make more sense. The Wave+ is also heavier than minimalist models, and there’s a learning curve when figuring out where everything lives.

Don’t forget that a premium multi-tool only represents good value if you look after it. We remove dirt after outdoor adventures and dry and lubricate it before storing. We also avoid forcing it to tackle jobs better suited to full-size tools. I wouldn’t, for example, choose its compact saw over a dedicated full-size version for pruning substantial tree branches in my yard.

If you’re using a Wave+ in the UK, like me, be aware of the country’s knife laws. You need a “good reason” to carry it in public because its blades lock. However, Emanuel explains that the legal language is ambiguous, so you shouldn’t assume you can carry one wherever you go just because it’s part of a multi-tool.

The Wave+ has convinced me that a good multi-tool is more than merely an expensive gimmick. It may not replace dedicated tools, but having so many functions at my fingertips in a form that is so compact, portable and easy to use makes it a practical, worthwhile investment.

The Wave Plus is a multi-tool workhorse. It packs 18 tools in one, including sharp blades, spring scissors, wire cutters, and more.

#7800. 3 Winterization Projects That Are as Easy as Painting

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 11, 2026 10:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Winter weather can be devastating to outdoor furniture, appliances, and structures, which is why many people store as much as possible in a covered shed or garage throughout the cold season. Even though not everything can be neatly tucked away, such as your deck, walkways, and gates, you can take steps to prepare them for harsh winter conditions before snow starts to fall.

Outdoor winterization projects that involve painting, staining, or sealing help surfaces create a durable barrier against freeze-thaw cycles, moisture intrusion, and corrosive deicing salts. It’s important to complete these protective jobs before the first hard freeze so you can prevent deep structural damage during the winter months.

Leaving wood decks, fences, or patio furniture bare during winter allows moisture from snow and ice to seep into the wood pores. When trapped water freezes, it expands, causing the wood to split, warp, and rot. A fresh coat of waterproof sealant or oil-based stain acts as a hydrophobic barrier. Water pools on top of the sealed surface rather than penetrating the wood grain.

Before applying a compatible exterior stain or water-repellent finish, clean the surface, remove failing finish, and allow the wood to dry sufficiently. For decking and steps, choose a winterization product specifically approved for horizontal surfaces and foot traffic.

Marc Sharkey, owner of Dynamic Painting Inc, says that “the finish reduces water absorption from rain and melting snow. Repeated wetting and drying can contribute to checking, splitting, and warping; prolonged dampness also creates conditions for decay.

“Pay particular attention to exposed board ends and areas where the old finish has worn away.” He also warns: “A new coating cannot repair rotten wood.” Given that Sharkey’s business is based in Alberta, he has experience dealing with some of the harshest winters in North America.

This oil-based formula provides corrosion resistance and weather protection for outdoor metal surfaces . Learn more in our buyer’s guide.

Winter preparation is important to safeguard your home. Chipped paint on steel or iron railings, furniture, and gates exposes the raw metal to oxygen and winter humidity, rapidly accelerating the oxidation process. Road salt or salt-based sidewalk ice melts further expedite this corrosion, eating through the metal structures. Applying a coat of exterior, rust-resistant enamel or oil-based paint seals out moisture and oxygen, halting the chemical reaction that creates rust.

It’s a budget-friendly winterization project that also forms a slick, chemical-resistant barrier against salt splash-back. Before applying a coating, remove loose rust and flaking paint and clean away dirt and salt. Then apply an appropriate rust-inhibiting primer and exterior metal finish. Check compatibility carefully: steel, aluminum, and galvanized metal can require different preparation and primers.

“An intact coating limits exposure to moisture and oxygen, helping slow corrosion. Left exposed, rust can spread beneath surrounding paint, causing more peeling and pitting. Over time, severe corrosion can weaken components. Painting over loose rust does not solve the underlying problem,” explains Sharkey.

Moisture from ice and snow can cause significant damage to concrete because it is a highly porous material. When snow melts on walkways, driveways, or patios, the concrete absorbs the water. Subsequent freezing temperatures cause that internal water to expand, which leads to surface flaking, scaling, and deep cracking.

Unlike surface coatings, penetrating sealers chemically bond inside concrete pores. They create an invisible, breathable hydrophobic barrier that prevents liquid water from sinking into the stone, while still allowing internal vapor to escape.

Sharkey notes that “for compatible, absorbent concrete steps, walkways, or patios, a penetrating sealer rated for exterior concrete and freeze-thaw exposure can reduce water absorption. Confirm compatibility with any existing treatment and follow the preparation instructions.”

Reducing water and deicing-salt penetration helps protect against winter deterioration. However, just keep in mind that a sealer is preventive maintenance; it does not repair cracks, failing concrete, or drainage problems.

#7798. Three men charged in $130M AI impersonation scheme

Three foreign nationals are accused of using artificial intelligence to pose as corporate executives and lawyers in a fraud scheme that allegedly took in over $129 million. (Image from Shutterstock)

Federal prosecutors in Manhattan have unsealed an indictment accusing three foreign nationals of using artificial intelligence to pose as corporate executives and lawyers in a fraud scheme that allegedly took in over $129 million, according a story published Friday in The Guardian.

According to the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit manipulated voices and images to deceive employees at companies around the world between 2024 and 2026. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain this summer, and Sheetrit was taken into custody in the United Kingdom in September.

According to prosecutors, the scheme worked in two stages. First, the defendants allegedly posed as a company executive and told employees they needed help with a confidential financial matter. Employees were then directed to contact attorneys at a major international law firm, whom the defendants also allegedly impersonated, and to wire large sums as instructed.

Prosecutors allege that the defendants stole nearly $5 million from a Missouri hospital system, about $2.7 million from a Rhode Island bank, roughly $3 million from a California hospital system, more than $4.6 million from a Massachusetts mutual fund, about $5 million from a Florida pet food company, and over $11 million from a U.K. technology company. The defendants have been indicted on charges relating to wire fraud, money laundering, conspiracy and identity theft.

Funds were allegedly routed to accounts in countries including the U.S., Spain, Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China, then converted to cryptocurrency to hide their origin and split among conspirators. Prosecutors say Soall and Hazan used several aliases, including “Rocky Balboa,” “Superman Cash” and “Ron.”

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement that while AI holds great promise, it can also be turned to criminal ends.

#7797. 8 Reasons a Contractor Might Give You an Outrageously High Estimate

If you just got a quote for a home repair that made your eyes water, there's probably a reason it's so high. A team of contractors weighs in with possible explanations.

If you just got a quote from a contractor that was way more than you thought it would be, join the club…it happens to the best of us. In fact, it’s a pretty common occurrence. Sometimes, though, the quote is so high that you can feel your mouth forming words you shouldn’t be saying. As someone who has been on both sides of such interactions, I can say that contractors don’t like them any more than you do. They know you can shop around, and they need your business. So what’s the deal with ridiculously high quotes?

I didn’t find any shortage of contractors willing to weigh in on this topic — one that is near and dear to their professional hearts. If a quote just made you hyperventilate, take a deep breath and check out some of the possible reasons why it’s so much higher than you expected.

“If an HVAC unit has a defective part that needs replacement, most of my clients will immediately ask how much the replacement part costs,” says HVAC technician Tamer Sayed. “I always tell the current market price and the misunderstanding often starts here. A few clients forget to take into account the labor and consultation fees. They assume they only had to pay for the replacement part.”

The same thing can happen with plumbing and electrical jobs. The part needed to get things working again may be small and inexpensive, and it may only account for a small portion of the quote. Sometimes the labor quote seems excessive, and that’s usually because the client doesn’t understand what’s involved with the repair.

Jake Vincett, a builder from the UK, makes this observation: “A lot of the time, the customer is comparing quotes for different work, because the cheaper one has included a surface repair whereas the more expensive one has quoted for fixing the underlying problem…It’s common that the customer doesn’t know or consider the amount of work going into a project. A new driveway isn’t just laying tarmac – it’s digging out the old one, laying the sub base, etc.”

Plumbing, electrical and HVAC expert Bob Cardwell adds: “It’s often not only one problem to fix but a bunch of small fixes. Even though it might be possible to fix the original problem without addressing the additional issues, an experienced and reliable technician will not ignore them, will try to fix them and will discuss them with the homeowner.”

Failing to provide a quote that addresses underlying issues and then delivering a sky-high bill at the end doesn’t just make the customer unhappy, says HVAC and plumbing expert Ryan Osterkamp. “It can make them feel like we don’t know what we’re doing.”

Osterkamp is used to hearing customers say: “I can go get that part for $X at Home Depot.” What they aren’t thinking about is the amount of training and expertise that made it possible for our technician to quickly and accurately diagnose the issue, have the supplies they need in their truck and be able to do the repair same day. Sure, you may save money by going with the guy on Facebook that works out of an old, unlabeled truck, but if his work doesn’t hold up, will he fix it without giving you the runaround? Is he insured? Does he offer a warranty?”

Tariffs, inflation and the economy in general are pushing prices up, and the dollar has lost a lot of its purchasing power for the average American. The same is true for contractors. “The fact of the matter is, we’re working harder now and making less,” says remodeling contractor Kevin Cullen. “In today’s economy, a lot of people are chasing the price to the bottom and shopping for the cheapest number. Unfortunately, they usually get what they pay for.”

A contractor who knows problems might creep up, such as a rotten subfloor that needs replacement during a toilet repair, makes an effort to warn customers as part of the quote. Potential problems aren’t always obvious. “There are times,” says Nika Tveretinova, who operates an HVAC business in Sacramento, “when the actual fix isn’t that complicated, but it’s the access that makes things tough—especially with equipment installed in an attic or cramped quarters. Sometimes we also find an old installation that needs a safety or code correction before we can put everything back together.”

In such situations, a higher-than-expected quote that you can reject is far better than a higher-than-expected bill you have to pay because the work is already completed.

Joshua Kurz founded NumeralQ, a home improvement pricing guide, and he cautions against comparing a bid you receive from a contractor to information you find online. “Owners often find an estimate online, and rather than waiting for a bid, they assume that number will be the actual cost. These estimates are helpful when determining a budget, but they are not interchangeable for actual bids. A 1,500 sq ft roof in one market will not necessarily cost the same in another market, and bids can even differ for neighboring houses.”

If you find a guy on Facebook who charges a low price to do a repair, there’s no guarantee that the repair will last or be up to code. When that person makes a mistake, a licensed contractor working on the same system at a later date might have to fix it, especially when inspectors are involved.

“Over a 40-year career,” says Cullen, “I’ve found many surprises: unsupported headers, no king or jack studs, undersized headers, poorly installed headers that aren’t flush and have gaps, termite damage, carpenter ant damage, water damage, mold. That’s not every job, but you never know when a homeowner bought a house in which a Rube Goldberg did the work on it.”

Sometimes a house is in such poor condition that a small repair, such as stopping a plumbing leak, can turn into a major project that involves replacing pipes, walls or subfloors. Rather than simply declining the repair, some contractors will offer a ridiculously high quote to avoid falling into a sinkhole of extra work. If the customer accepts the quote, the contractor won’t lose money by taking the job. A customer who rejects a bid can keep shopping with no harm done.

After researching and comparing product features and reviews for dozens of nonstick snow blower sprays, we narrowed our testing list to eight products. As our property in Montana got hit with one winter storm after another, we had plenty of snow to work through as well as very cold weather, so we got to work lubricating several gas snow blowers, cordless snow blowers, and electric snow blowers with each of our chosen products.

A large portion of our work coincided with our tests on snow blowers for gravel driveways, meaning the sprays were all used in particularly rough conditions since the snow contained dirt and hard particles. We also tested them on shovels, plow blades, door locks, and other surfaces needing lubrication to get a comprehensive idea of how long each spray remained effective, their ease of application, and their overall performance.

Before choosing a nonstick spray, take a few minutes to learn what to look for, including drying time, safety concerns, functions, and the spray’s longevity.

The drying time for a spray wax for snow blowers will vary depending on the specific product, the temperature and humidity of the environment, and the moisture content in the snow blower’s chute. Products that dry quickly are generally easier to use since they make applying a second layer when needed faster so you can get to work sooner.

Applying the nonstick snow and ice repellent in a warm, dry environment, like a garage or workshop, is ideal. Warmth helps the spray stick to the metal and dry quickly. Users can apply sprays to damp surfaces in freezing temperatures, but it will take longer for the spray to dry. Until the spray is completely dry, it won’t lubricate properly, nor will it be fully water- or corrosion-resistant.

While nonstick sprays for snow blowers are helpful in preventing clogs, they often contain chemicals that warrant handling them with care. We recommend you check the product’s label for safe application recommendations and to see if it contains any hazardous materials.

Generally speaking, you’ll want to keep snow blower sprays out of reach of children and pets since they can be toxic if ingested or inhaled. It’s a good idea to use these products in a well-ventilated space and consider wearing eye protection, a respirator, and gloves. Because the liquid spray may be flammable until it dries, store it away from sources of heat or flames.

The primary purpose of a nonstick spray for snow blowers is to lubricate the inside of the snow blower chute to keep snow from sticking and clogging the chute. However, many nonstick sprays have additional benefits, such as preventing rust, protecting against ultraviolet (UV) damage, resisting water, or even adding a shine to metal finishes.

Longevity refers to the length of time a nonstick spray remains effective after application. Every nonstick spray we tested must be reapplied frequently, though some worked well through several uses. Generally speaking, they all need to be reapplied every few uses at a minimum.

When working through a really difficult storm, consider reapplying nonstick spray after every use to keep the machine performing optimally. Always apply a fresh coat ahead of storms and continue renewing the coating as needed throughout the season. Even if you go through a couple of cans in the winter, you will still save money removing snow yourself rather than paying the cost of professional snow removal.

Learn more about nonstick spray for snow blowers by reading the answers to these frequently asked questions.

Snow blower chutes can clog because you’re trying to push through the snow too fast. They also clog when the heavy snow has a high moisture content and forms compact clumps that stick to the sides of the chute.

You can use normal WD-40 to help lubricate the auger and moving parts on a snow blower. Use the silicone version of the product to add a nonstick layer of protection on the snow blower chute and auger. It’s easy to apply, dries quickly, and acts as a water repellent and corrosion inhibitor.

Snow blower spray is easy to use: Just shake the can, remove the lid, and spray an even coating inside the chute and to the auger. The nonstick spray lubricant makes the chute and auger slippery, preventing snow from sticking and clogging the blower.

For a complete set of instructions regarding snow blower maintenance, see our guide on how to maintain a snow blower. While the specific maintenance steps your machine requires will depend on the type of snow blower you have, general steps include checking all fittings and components, changing oil or charging batteries, and lubricating the drive and chassis.

#7795. What Those Little Holes in Your Plug Prongs Are Actually For

Those little holes in electrical plug prongs have a purpose, but it isn't what most people think. Here's why they're still there.

Not all electronic cords look the same. Some have two prongs; others have three or even four. Some have prongs at weird angles, or are even designed for orange electrical outlets. Odds are most people have also seen electrical prongs with holes in them, but the reason for them isn’t common knowledge.

Those two tiny circles often appear near the ends of the metal blades, and newer outlets no longer depend on them. Learn how the feature started, why some manufacturers still use them, what homeowners should know about plug safety, and more.

The holes originally helped keep plugs from slipping out of outlets. Some older outlets had small bumps inside that fit into the holes when someone plugged something in. That changed when Underwriters Laboratories began requiring outlets to hold plugs securely without those bumps.

“Most manufacturers stopped putting the detent nibs on the female contacts, as it made it much harder to meet the maximum force to withdraw and did nothing for the minimum requirement, as the gage had no holes,” according to the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA).

Basically, the bumps made plugs harder to remove, so manufacturers stopped using them. Today, outlets grip the prongs instead. If a plug starts slipping out, the outlet may need to be replaced. The holes aren’t a child safety feature, either. Tamper-resistant outlets use built-in shutters to keep children from sticking objects inside.

“TRRs work like normal outlets,” according to the Electrical Safety Foundation International. “When you plug into a TRR for the first time, you may be able to feel the internal shutter system engaging. If excessive force is needed to insert a plug into a TRR, there’s a chance that the plug, not the receptacle, is damaged.”

Manufacturers sometimes use the holes to hold the metal prongs in place while making plugs. They don’t help electricity flow through the plug, though. The holes can also hold small safety tags or locks on unplugged appliances. However, these shouldn’t replace proper safety equipment. OSHA also has rules for preventing equipment from accidentally starting during certain types of workplace maintenance.

The holes aren’t even required under American electrical plug standards. Manufacturers can make plugs without them, although NEMA has rules for their size and placement when included. They also have nothing to do with grounding. On a three-prong plug, the round prong handles that job. The two flat prongs work the same way whether they have holes or not.

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”

“By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution.  We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”

“The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” said Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

#7791. Elon Musk Is Pulling the Plug on Cybertrucks to Focus on Something New

Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production next year as Elon Musk shifts attention to its Cybercab. Here's what the change means.

Tesla Cybertrucks have dominated headlines even before they hit the road. But now it appears their time in the automotive world spotlight might be coming to an end. The company’s CEO Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory to make room for the Cybercab, the company’s self-driving taxi.

Learn why the company is changing direction and what the news means for the Cybertruck.

Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images

In a Nov. 6 post on X, Musk wrote, “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

Tesla began delivering Cybertrucks in late 2023, but sales haven’t lived up to expectations. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates published by Cox Automotive, U.S. sales fell by nearly half in 2025. The truck has also faced criticism for its price, design, and quality issues, as well as several safety recalls.

Current owners can continue driving their Cybertrucks, and existing warranty terms still apply. Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill also addressed concerns about future repairs. “Tesla will maintain spare parts and service will continue support,” he wrote on X on November 6. He didn’t specify how long that support would last.

For anyone still waiting on a Cybertruck, the news is less encouraging. In a Nov. 9 post on X, Musk wrote, “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”

Tesla hasn’t said which customers will receive their trucks or how it plans to handle the remaining orders.

The Cybercab is Tesla’s two-seat electric car designed to drive itself. It doesn’t have a steering wheel or pedals because it won’t need a human driver. Tesla has already started offering Cybercab rides in parts of Austin. The company plans to expand the service, although the vehicles aren’t widely available yet.

Musk denies that Tesla is ending production because the Cybertruck isn’t profitable. He says the company can put its Texas factory to better use by making Cybercabs.

Following a few energy-saving strategies when setting the temperature on your thermostat can make a big difference in winter. According to the U.S. Department of Energy, it’s possible to save 10 percent a year on energy bills by being conservative with thermostat settings year-round.

We consulted an HVAC expert about thermostat-setting strategies during the coldest months of the year, and how we can save on energy costs. Here’s what he said.

“I prefer setting the thermostat to around 68 degrees Fahrenheit (20 degrees Celsius) during the day. This temperature strikes a balance between comfort and energy efficiency,” says Josh Mitchell, HVAC technician and founder of Air Conditioner Lab. “At night, lowering it to about 65 degrees Fahrenheit (18 degrees Celsius) is comfortable for sleeping and helps save on heating costs.”

According to the Department of Energy, setting your thermostat to the lowest comfortable temperature, which is typically 68 degrees Fahrenheit in the winter, helps slow down heat loss for homes with a regular furnace or baseboard heating system. However, that’s not the case for homes with heat pumps. Dialing down the thermostat too much can make a heat pump less efficient.

Everyone has a different comfort zone when it comes to temperatures. Just because 68 degrees can be an ideal temperature for a house in terms of reducing energy consumption doesn’t mean it’s right for everyone. Some people may prefer to set the thermostat slightly higher, at 70 degrees, and that’s okay.

The  Amazon Smart Thermostat uses Alexa to adjust the thermostat based on whether it thinks you’re home. Read the review.

It’s important to install a thermostat in the right location to prevent inaccurate temperature readings. Called ‘ghost readings,’ a thermostat may be triggered to run unnecessarily if placed near drafts, sunlight, and doorways. If air flow near the thermostat is blocked by furniture, also may not run effectively.

Mitchell says that the best place to locate a thermostat is on an interior wall that experiences the natural air flow in the home and is away from direct sunlight, drafts, doorways, and windows.

Your body requires time to adapt to slightly cooler temperatures. So there’s no need to (literally) go cold turkey when cooler outdoor temps arrive. Lower the temperature gradually, so you have time to adjust to being a little chilly. Until you acclimate, wear layers, don warm socks, and have a snuggly blanket on hand.

Regardless of how low you set the thermostat, you won’t save on your heating bill if your furnace or heating system works inefficiently. Make sure to do the following:

“Setting the thermostat too high in winter can lead to excessive energy consumption and higher utility bills,” Mitchell explains. “Conversely, setting it too low might not provide adequate comfort and could even risk pipes freezing. The key is to find a balanced setting that ensures comfort without overburdening your heating system.”

Consider investing in a programmable thermostat that’ll automatically adjust the temperature for you. Programmable thermostats are ideal for people with consistent schedules.

“I’m a strong advocate for smart thermostats,” Mitchell says. “They offer advanced features like learning your schedule, remote control via a smartphone app, and energy usage reports, which not only enhances energy efficiency but also contributes to a more comfortable living environment.”

If your day-to-day routine is a bit more haphazard than a regular 9 to 5, consider a smart thermostat. Helpful features of some smart thermostats include settings that automatically detect your absence and lower the thermostat temperature while you’re gone. Some units can adjust the indoor temperature based on weather data.

“The ability to monitor and adjust your home’s temperature settings from anywhere can lead to cost savings and reduce your carbon footprint,” Mitchell explains.

Unless you work from home, turning the thermostat down during the workday can mean big savings on your energy bill. If you have pets, of course, you’ll want to set the thermostat to a temperature that will keep them comfortable while you’re gone. Still, the exact comfort zone will vary depending on the kind of pet and the animal’s size.

Another good opportunity to lower your thermostat is while you sleep. After all, research suggests that most people sleep poorly in overly warm conditions.

#7789. 15 Things You Should Never Burn in the Fireplace

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 12, 2026 10:44 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Thanks to modern heating technologies, homeowners today no longer have to rely on fire for heat. But that doesn’t mean a crackling fire in the fireplace isn’t a wonderful antidote to a cold evening, and more and more are embracing this cozy heating method. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the number of fireplaces built in single-family homes has been steadily increasing over the last decade. And Verified Market Research says the wood stoves market size was valued at $8.35 billion in 2025 and projected to reach $14.89 billion by 2033.

Be smart, however, about what you toss on the fire; some combustibles can cause immediate danger, such as serious respiratory reactions, or contribute to long-term problems, such as creosote buildup, which can lead to chimney fires.

When you burn coated or pressure-treated wood, toxic chemicals can be released into the air you breathe. For example, wood treated to withstand rot or insects used to contain a form of arsenic, and painted, stained, or varnished woods contain other chemicals—and all these chemicals create toxic fumes when burned. Nix on plywood, too, because adhesives applied during manufacturing release toxic fumes when burned.

Treated lumber often has a stamp or a tag on it to indicate it’s been altered, but of course, those might be missing from scrap lumber. Look for a green or blue tint or an oily feel—or simply err on the side of caution and refrain from burning any lumber in your fireplace.

Small recyclables are often used to start a roaring fire because they usually catch fire quickly. The next time you need to get a fire going, however, don’t use cardboard, which is often treated with chemicals, dyes, and glues. Additionally, burning cardboard bits can often float out of the fire and onto your carpet or furniture. Instead, use approved fire starters, available from camping-supply stores, or small splinters of wood, chipped with an ax from your stock of seasoned firewood.

Odorless, nontoxic, and eco-friendly, Superior Trading’s fire starters are made of food-grade wax and wood shavings. Read the review.

Never use lighter fluid, charcoal starter fluid, or any other type of accelerant to start a fire in a fireplace. These products should not be used to fuel an indoor fire, in part because they often contain methanol and petroleum-based chemicals that produce toxic fumes. In addition, the use of accelerants creates an extra-hot fire that can damage your chimney liner.

RELATED: The Best Fire Logs for Long-Lasting Ambience, Tested

The inks used to create colorful magazine layouts contain chemical pigments that release toxic fumes when burned. You may instead use a couple of sheets (not more) of plain black-and-white newspaper, rolled tightly and placed beneath small bits of wood kindling, but don’t toss magazines, gift wrap, or coupon inserts into the fireplace. Not only do these items create unwanted fumes, but bits of burning paper can float up and out of an uncapped chimney, putting your roof and nearby structures at risk of fire.

RELATED: The Best Creosote Removers to Keep Your Chimney Clean

The best thing you can do to make sure your firewood is always fireplace-ready is to keep it dry. For starters, dry wood is easier to light than damp wood. Even more important, the moisture in wet firewood makes it smoke and leads to rapid creosote buildup in the chimney liner. In fact, creosote buildup is a leading cause of chimney fires. While you can’t completely avoid creosote, you can reduce the risk of buildup by burning only dry firewood and having your chimney cleaned annually.

This creosote remover dissolves first- and second-degree creosote in your chimney, turning it into ash. Read our full review.

You wouldn’t intentionally roll around in a patch of poison oak, but you’ll put your whole family at risk if you burn the woody vines from poison sumac, poison ivy, or plants that contain urushiol, a toxic irritant that causes rashes on contact. In winter, when plants lose their leaves, it can be difficult to tell if you’re gathering harmless vines or poisonous ones, so take precautions by avoiding anything you can’t identify. The reason? Fumes from burning plants that contain urushiol can trigger serious allergic respiratory reactions.

Evergreen trees, such as pine, spruce, and cedar (yes, even your old Christmas tree), contain resins that catch fire quickly and produce a hot flame. While this might sound good, these trees burn so fast that the fire will fizzle out quickly, and their high resin content can leave heavy creosote deposits in your chimney, which can over time lead to chimney fires.

Finding a way to repurpose wood shipping pallets is a great idea—just don’t burn them. Discarded shipping pallets are popular materials for resourceful DIYers and crafters, but many pallets have been treated with the chemical pesticide methyl bromide to prevent the spread of the emerald ash borer, a beetle that wreaks havoc on living ash trees. Never burn a pallet that bears the stamp “MB,” which indicates that it has been treated with chemicals. Even if you don’t see a stamp, it’s probably safest to avoid burning pallets altogether.

If you’ve ever attended a beach party where driftwood was burned, you probably marveled at the beautiful lavender-blue flames. Those colorful flames are produced by metal salts that the wood absorbed while it was adrift, and, unfortunately, the fumes from those flames are toxic. Many seaside communities have banned the burning of driftwood for just that reason, so follow their lead and don’t burn wood that you’ve gathered on the beach in your fireplace.

Most consumer products contain chemicals that produce hazardous fumes when burned. What’s worse? Some of the most toxic trash items contain plastic, which releases a category of toxins known as dioxins. Inhaling dioxins increases the risk of respiratory ailments, headaches, internal organ damage, and even cancer. And as we said before, lightweight bits of burning material can float out of the fireplace and onto surfaces in your home—not good!

Starting a fire at home with a base of dried leaves might seem like a good way to put fallen leaves to use, but it’s not. First, leaves burn very quickly and hot. This sudden and extreme change in temperature can crack chimney flues and masonry, which is why it’s best to get your fireplace going with a chimney starter instead. Wet leaves will do the opposite, burning slowly while smoldering and creating a ton of smoke. That smoke generates creosote buildup, which can cause chimney fires.

Many folks like adding scents to their fireplace, opting for the fresh aromas of oranges, lemons, apples, and the like. The problem is that fresh, moist fruit peels will smolder in a fire, and lead to abundant smoke and creosote buildup. A better course of action is to dry your fruit peels at a low temperature in the oven, and then toss them on your fire. You’ll still get a fresh scent, but not the moisture.

RELATED: 20 Crazy Cleaning Tips That Actually Work

Believe it or not, decades ago magazine ads actually encouraged homeowners to burn batteries in their fireplaces because burning zinc was believed to prevent creosote formation (burning batteries also resulted in a rainbow of beautiful colors). While that might’ve been true, modern batteries will explode under extreme heat and potentially cause severe chemical burns. Beyond the potential burns, fumes from burning chemicals are also poisonous. Instead, it’s best to dispose of batteries the right way.

It might seem like a good idea to throw old T-shirts, rags, and other fabric in a fireplace to start a fire, but you’d be wrong. Cloth and clothing will create a nasty smell as well as a ton of smoke as it smolders. That smoke will coat the inside of the chimney with creosote, which can cause chimney fires. A better course of action is to pack those old shirts up and drop them off at the local homeless shelter or SPCA.

RELATED: How to Get Your Fireplace Ready for Winter

Anyone who’s seen the red-hot glow in the bottom of a charcoal grill knows that charcoal can create a ton of heat. It also produces carbon monoxide, which isn’t as dangerous in the open air as it is indoors. However, if there’s too much draft the charcoal can burn twice as hot as wood, which could damage the chimney or flue. For that reason, charcoal’s best left for summer grilling outdoors.

While the fireplace is not the best disposal solution for most household trash, there are a few items you can safely dispose of in the fireplace rather than sending them to the landfill:

#7788. What Should You Do With Pumpkins After Halloween?

Should you compost pumpkins after Halloween, toss them in the trash or leave them out for wildlife? Experts explain the options.

Before they migrated to North America, the Irish and Scottish immigrants who established the tradition of jack-o’-lanterns, carved turnips. In the New World, they started carving pumpkins, which were readily available and far more dramatic. Since then, the Halloween tradition they established in the 19th century has only grown more popular and sees more and more pumpkins discarded every year.

How many? “One billion (with a B!),” exclaims composter Lauren Click, and that’s not good, because not everyone responsibly disposes of their jack-o’-lanterns responsibly.

If you care about soil, wildlife and the environment in general, there really is a right way and a wrong way to dispose of pumpkins after Halloween. A gardening expert, a composting expert and a worm farmer explain the difference.

Definitely, yes. “There are many ways to compost a pumpkin,” says Click. “I chop mine up into smaller pieces and feed it to my indoor worm compost farm. You can compost all parts of a pumpkin as long as it is not treated with chemicals, has no paint (so, no painted pumpkins), no glitter, and no plastic/wax/metal candle residue. You can even compost moldy/gross pumpkins!”

It’s important to chop up the pumpkin and not throw it on the compost pile whole, adds UK gardener David Denyer. “Pumpkins decompose slowly if left whole because of their thick rind and high water content. Because of this, adding them straight to your compost can throw off the balance, making the heap turn slimy or even anaerobic, which stops it from breaking down properly.”

One option is to give them to animal rescues and local farmers to use as feed for pigs, chickens and livestock. Click loves this option because, as she says, many farmers compost manure, which makes it a win-win situation. The pumpkin winds up providing nourishment in the soil for more pumpkins.

If you live in the city, worm farmer Scott Kent has another suggestion: “Take your leftover pumpkins is to a worm farm! Composting worms, like red wigglers, consume organic waste and create worm castings from it. Pumpkins, and most all other cucurbits for that matter, are among composting worms’ most favorite foods.”

For a quick way to recycle pumpkins after Halloween that you can do at home, cut the pumpkin into small chunks and bury them in your garden. “This works like a green manure,” says Denyer, “adding organic matter below the surface where it can decompose safely without attracting any pests or spreading disease.”

This is generally a bad idea, say our experts. Click worries about attracting wildlife to areas in which they can be harmed, but beyond that, decomposing pumpkins are not the best source of nutrition. “The acidity and mold that develops as they rot can make hedgehogs, insects, and birds unwell,” says Denyer, who lives where hedgehogs are a thing.

The danger to wildlife increases if the pumpkin contains toxic materials. If you wouldn’t feed, paint, glitter or candle wax to a pet, you shouldn’t feed it to wildlife.

Before carving a pumpkin, most people remove the seeds. Don’t throw them out. When you roast them, they make a delicious snack. After the seeds are gone, the rind makes a good (if temporary) planter for displaying your fall blooms on the porch. Just remember to line the inside to prevent dirt from spilling out from the face you carved.

Composting may be the best way to recycle a pumpkin rind, but if you’re okay with a less dramatic jack-o’-lantern, a smaller pumpkin like a Hokkaido or Baby-Bear can serve a double purpose. Unlike large carving pumpkins with thick, waxy skins, these smaller varieties have thin skins and a high sugar content that make them delicious in soup.

Don’t just toss  them in the garden, warns Denyer: “Pumpkins are high in water and sugars, which means they quickly break down into a thick, slimy layer that blocks air circulation and traps moisture around plant roots. This can then encourage fungal problems, like grey mold or powdery mildew, which can spread to nearby plants.”

It’s important to check with the local waste management rules, because some communities don’t allow pumpkins in yard waste bins. If your community allows them, remove candle wax and other inorganic materials.

Painted pumpkins present a problem: They are organic, but because of the paint, you shouldn’t throw them in organic waste, and some communities prohibit organic materials in the general trash. In such cases, cutting up and burying your pumpkins after Halloween is probably the best solution.

If you leave a whole pumpkin out in the field, it will start decomposing about eight or 12 weeks after it’s fully ripe. Once you cut a pumpkin into smaller pieces and throw them in a compost pile, the pieces will start to rot in five to 10 days.

Full decomposition depends on the moisture content of the air and soil, and on the temperature. It occurs faster when there’s lots of moisture and the air is warm.

Generally, no. Most paints contain toxic chemicals that can poison the compost and the soil on which you spread it. This isn’t necessarily true for all paints, including some water-soluble plant- or egg-based children’s paints, but if you don’t know where the paint came from, keep the painted pumpkin out of the compost.

A paint may be safe for kids, but that doesn’t mean it’s safe for composting. Crayola, a manufacturer of safe-to-use paints for children, recommends using them on pumpkins but warns that those pumpkins should not be consumed (meaning they should not go in the compost).

#7786. Former U.S. Government Contractor Arrested for Allegedly Leaking National Defense Information and Stealing Night Vision Goggles

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

Ashbacher was charged by an indictment unsealed Tuesday with unlawfully transmitting and retaining national defense information and with theft of government property.

According to the indictment, beginning in or about 2021, the defendant worked as an employee of a private company that provided security and emergency management services at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command facility in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. To perform the required functions of his employment, Ashbacher held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

As further detailed in the indictment, Ashbacher photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other users to a second social media site. Ashbacher asked a social media user in a private message to remove some materials and further stated that he was “trying to do some damage control.” A search of Ashbacher’s residence also revealed a classified award write-up that contained additional national defense information, along with a night vision goggle system specific to a military unit within Army Special Operations Command that had been reported missing.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

Trial Attorney Leslie Esbrook of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Logan Liles for the Eastern District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7785. The Right Types of Christmas Lights for Indoor and Outdoor Holiday Displays

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Deirdre Mundorf, Updated by Margaret Foley

Updated Nov 12, 2026 11:41 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Each year, as the holiday season approaches, homeowners prepare to deck their homes in sparkling lights. They pull tangled strings from their attics and garages and then, after rushing to the store for replacement bulbs, fuses, or even more lights, they get to work. But if they’re starting fresh in a new house or trying to change up their holiday decor, they have some lighting decisions to make: What kind of Christmas lights should they use? What are the best Christmas lights for the roof? Which lights should are best for the mantel?

More than 150 million strings of Christmas lights are sold in the U.S. every year. Homeowners certainly have a lot to choose from. This guide is the place to start. Here you’ll find some Christmas light basics, a review of the most common types of lights, and suggestions for the best uses for each type.

First, decide whether you want LED or incandescent lights. The choice largely comes down to cost, energy efficiency, and aesthetics.

Since their introduction in the late 1990s, LED Christmas lights have become increasingly popular. In 2024, LED lights accounted for more than 90 percent of holiday string light sales, and for good reason. LED Christmas lights are far more energy efficient and last significantly longer than incandescent bulbs, going strong for upwards of 50,000 hours. Additionally, LED bulbs are brighter and stay cooler than incandescent bulbs. Also worth noting: While you can generally connect only three or so incandescent light strings together, you can link together many more LED strings, depending on their wattage. This can be a big help if you’re installing lights along an expansive roof or trimming an especially large tree.

LEDs do, however, have some significant negatives. For starters, they cost more than incandescents. However, because they last longer and are more energy efficient, the higher expense can be offset over time by lower utility costs and savings from not having to replace the lights as frequently. Another drawback: Some homeowners simply don’t like the look of LEDs, finding the light too harsh and their colors too cool. While newer LEDs have a greater range of color temperature and improved color rendering, some shoppers still prefer the cozier look of incandescents.

Best For: Those willing to pay a higher upfront cost in return for energy efficiency and a vibrant display.

Our Recommendation: Connectable 240 LED Twinkle Fairy Light String at Amazon for $17.99These LED wide-angle indoor/outdoor lights extend to a length of 88 feet, offer 13 lighting modes, and are available in a range of colors.

Incandescent lights are typically less expensive than LEDs and emit a warmer, softer glow. However, incandescent bulbs burn out faster, are less durable, and consume a lot more electricity than LED bulbs.

Best For: Creating a nostalgic display with a warmer, cozier glow.

Our Recommendation: Home Accents Holiday 300 Incandescent Mini String Lights at The Home Depot for $9.98Even if one of the bulbs burns out, this 68-foot strand of 300 mini incandescent lights will stay lit; available in white and multicolor.

Holiday lights are rated for outdoor use, indoor use only, or indoor/outdoor use.

In a 2026 survey by Thumbtack, over half of respondents plan to hang holiday lights outdoors this year. If you’re part of this majority, be sure that you’re using outdoor-rated holiday lights for your outdoor Christmas light installations. These lights are more weather-resistant, have thicker wiring, and are made of more durable materials than indoor Christmas lights. Other tips for selecting and hanging outdoor lights include:

The Balsam Hill classic spruce tree is well-made, easy to set up, and sturdy enough to hang heavy ornaments. See our full review.

Christmas lights can be powered by electricity, batteries, solar energy, or even USB. Your budget and access to electrical outlets will help you determine which power sources are best for your situation.

Plug-in lights are any type of light that plugs into an electrical socket. This is the traditional way of powering Christmas lights.

For plug-in lights, you need a nearby electrical outlet or an extension cord. Once plugged in, the lights stay on as long as there’s power. There’s no need to worry about dead batteries or the solar charge depleting.

Best For: Creating dependable, long-lasting holiday light displays near a power outlet or where an extension cord can be used.

Our Recommendation: Prextex 100-Count White Christmas Lights at Amazon for $8.99This 20-foot incandescent light string has 100 warm white lights with a waterproof design suitable for indoor or outdoor use.

Some holiday lights rely on battery power, often using AA batteries. These sets are great solutions in situations where cords could pose a tripping hazard. where you want to keep the power source hidden, or where there are no electrical outlets nearby—for instance, if you want to add lights to a Christmas wreath on an entry door.

The lifespan of battery-operated lights can vary depending on the number of lights on the strand, whether the bulbs are LED or incandescent, the quality of the batteries, and other factors. While some lights may stay lit for more than 100 hours before requiring new batteries, others will need fresh batteries after only a few hours.

Best For: Displaying lights where no power outlets are available or where cords either aren’t wanted or can’t be used.

Our Recommendation: Loende Battery-Operated String Lights at Amazon for $12.99These classic-looking LED string lights are available in white, clear, and multicolor. The 50-light, 18-foot string features eight lighting modes and an automatic timer.

Solar-powered Christmas lights offer an eco-friendly solution for holiday decorations. Rather than consuming electricity, these lights are powered by sunlight through a connected solar panel. Solar Christmas lights are often comparably priced to their plug-in LED counterparts.

Though they’re eco-friendly, be forewarned that the lights may not stay lit very long at night if the solar panel doesn’t receive enough sunlight during the day. Also, if you’re planning a large display, the individual solar panels of each light strand could leave your lawn looking cluttered.

Best For: Small outdoor areas that get a lot of sunlight, such as sunny pathways, small sections of fence, and shrubs.

Our Recommendation: Joomer Solar Christmas Lights 2 Pack at Amazon for $19.99 Available in white and multicolor as well as several single-color options, this two-pack totals 400 LED lights and 144 feet and is safe for indoor and outdoor use. The strands offer eight lighting modes, and a 6-hour charge during the day will power the lights for more than 8 hours.

Plug these lights into a laptop, power bank, USB power adapter, or anywhere else you find a USB port. They’re handy for brightening up bedrooms, backyards, campsites, and other spots where a USB port is the most convenient power option.

Best For: Any space where a USB port is the most easily accessible power source for spreading some holiday cheer.

Our Recommendation: Green Convenience 100 LED USB or Battery String Lights at Amazon for $9.99This 33-foot indoor/outdoor holiday light string can be powered with either batteries or USB, offers eight lighting modes, comes with a remote control and timer function, and is available in white or multicolor.

Once you’ve decided whether you want LED or incandescent lights and have figured out how you’ll power them, it’s time to choose the best Christmas lights to suit your holiday decor. Here’s a rundown of the most common string and bulb styles and some of their best uses.

These small cylindrical bulbs with pointy tips are the most common holiday string lights. They’re available with both LED and incandescent bulbs and are sold for both indoor and outdoor use. Though they’re probably the most popular types of Christmas tree lights, mini string lights are also great for highlighting the mantel, wrapping around columns and banisters, and draping over entryways and windows. These are the light strings you’ll find crowding the shelves at the best places to find Christmas lights.

There are two main types of mini lights: M5 bulbs and T5 bulbs. Their shapes are similar, but T5 bulbs have a pointier tip, while M5 bulbs have a more rounded tip and textured sides.

Best For: Decorating Christmas trees and hanging over windows and entryways.

Our Recommendation: Minetom LED Christmas Mini Lights, Warm White at Amazon for $16.99Give a warm glow to your Christmas tree, bushes, columns, and more with this 75-foot string of 200 indoor/outdoor mini lights that offers eight lighting modes.

For a vintage look, nothing beats classic, colorful C6, C7, and C9 bulbs. Their rounded, conical shape evokes the homey Christmas trees in movies like It’s a Wonderful Life and A Christmas Story.

These days, C-type bulbs are available in both incandescent and LED light strings and in a range of colors. Use the smaller C6 (1⅛ inches tall) or C7 bulbs (1½ inches tall) indoors to give the Christmas tree or mantel a retro vibe, or outside on smaller trees and architectural features. The larger C9 bulbs (2½ inches tall) are best used outside to frame the roof or windows, or to wrap larger trees and shrubs.

C6 and C7, Best For: Lighting retro-style Christmas trees and smaller landscaping features.

Our Recommendation: Dazzle Bright C6 Christmas String Lights at Amazon for $16.99This set of indoor/outdoor C6 Christmas lights has 100 multicolor LED bulbs and eight lighting modes; UL-certified, and can be used indoors or outdoors.

Our Recommendation: Minetom C7 Christmas String Lights at Amazon for $33.99This 50-foot string has 52 C7 bulbs that are transparent, warm white, and give a vintage glow.

C9, Best For: Illuminating a large roofline.

Our Recommendation: Wintergreen 25 C9 Multicolor LED Christmas Lights at Amazon for $22.99This 17-foot string of faceted, indoor/outdoor C9 LED bulbs is expandable (you can safely connect up to 90 sets), long-lasting, and even dimmable.

Also known as 5mm lights, these bulbs have a concave lens that spreads extremely bright light in all directions. Because they’re compact, they don’t snag as easily as larger lights, so they’re often the bulb of choice for wrapping tree trunks and branches. Don’t let their small size fool you—these lights can easily illuminate large spaces.

Best For: Wrapping branches, bushes, or trees.

Our Recommendation: Wintergreen Lighting Multicolor 5mm LED Christmas Lights at Amazon for $24.99Available in white, single-color, and a variety of color combinations, this 24-foot strand of 70 LEDs is backed by a 3-year seasonal warranty—and you can string together 44 sets.

Strings of icicle lights have short, vertical strands of mini lights (or actual icicle-shaped bulbs) hanging down at intervals, “dripping” like icicles. They’re available in both LED and incandescent, and although white icicle lights are most popular, they’re also available in multicolor and single-color strands.

Best For: Installing on eaves to mimic dripping icicles.

Our Recommendation: Knonew Christmas Icicle Lights at Amazon for $69.99This 99-foot string of icicle lights features 228 vertical drops, eight modes, and a built-in timer. Also available in multicolor and single-color strands.

Pathway lights are mounted on stakes that can be driven into the ground along walkways, driveways, or garden beds to enhance safety and spread holiday joy. These eye-catching outdoor decorations are typically plug-in or solar-powered and available in fanciful shapes like candy canes, jolly Santas, and Christmas bulbs.

Best For: Lining front walkways or driveways.

Our Recommendation: Brightown C9 Christmas String Lights LED Pathway Lights at Amazon for $32.99With 20 C9 bulbs on a 25.7-foot string, these plug-in LED pathway lights will brighten up walkways and garden beds. They’re also available in faceted and multicolor styles.

Add a bright, modern, geometric touch to your outdoor decor with durable, flexible rope lights. They’re easy to bend around railings and columns, and some strands offer color-changing or chasing effects.

Best For: Wrapping tree trunks and banisters, and accenting architectural features.

Our Recommendation: Wintergreen Lighting 18-Foot LED Warm White Rope Lights at Amazon for $27.99The kit includes an 18-foot length of rope with 216 LED bulbs, mounting clips, three splice connectors, and end caps. Connect up to 15 kits; available in multicolor and various color combinations as well as single-color options.

Net lights are light strings that have been connected into a grid. They’re a hassle-free way to create a uniform blanket of light on bushes and hedges. Similarly, trunk lights are nets designed to wrap around the trunk of a tree. Both products can really speed up holiday decorating.

To make sure you’re buying the right size, first measure the square footage (surface area) of the shrub you’d like to cover. Net lights generally range from 4 to 10 feet long and 2 to 5 feet wide, although they can run much larger.

Best For: Covering shrubs and hedges with lights.

Our Recommendation: Meteds 120 LED Christmas Net Lights at Amazon for $23.39The warm white bulbs in this 6-by-4-foot net light will give your shrub a romantic glow, but it’s also available in cool white as well as three colorful options. Connect up to 10 sets.

Many of the LED light options in this list are available with color-changing features, where bulbs produce many different hues, or “chasing” features, where bulbs cycle on and off in patterns that create the illusion of lights moving along the string. These technological wonders may be the most fun and interactive types of Christmas tree lighting, and whether they’re used indoors or out, they give the homeowner the ability to customize or reimagine their holiday decorating scheme at a moment’s notice, often using a remote or an app.

Best For: Creating dynamic, customizable holiday light displays, indoors and outside.

For the Christmas tree: Plan on at least 100 lights per vertical foot of tree, more if the tree is especially wide or if you like a really bright tree.

For shrubs: Net lights are the fastest and easiest way to illuminate bushes. Just measure the approximate surface area of the bush and purchase a net light that will cover it. If you’re using string lights, figure 50 lights per square foot.

For the exterior: Decide where you want to install lights. Do you want them just along the eaves, or would you like to outline windows, railings, and other architectural features? Measure the total linear feet you intend to cover, add 10 percent to account for corners, plug-in space, and irregularities, and then divide by the length of your light strands (for example, 25 feet or 50 feet) to determine how many you’ll need.

For wrapping columns/tree trunks: The number of lights needed will vary depending on the circumference and height of the column, the desired vertical spacing of the lights, and the distance between lights on the string (for mini lights, the standard is 4 or 6 inches). To make things easier, check online for calculators.

#7784. Judge Richard Posner, RIP

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Posner was one of the greatest legal scholars of all time, a founder of law and economics, and an enormously influential judge.

Judge Richard Posner passed away yesterday. Posner was one of the greatest legal scholars of all time, one of the founders of the field of law and economics, and probably the most influential lower-court federal judge of the last several decades. His contributions across a wide range of fields are so great, that no obituary can possibly do them justice.

As a longtime professor at the University of Chicago Law School, Posner was a pioneer of the application of economics to legal issues. His book Economic Analysis of Law, (which has gone through numerous editions since the first one in 1973), was and is the best overview of the field. His classic articles on antitrust law, regulation, the economics of common law, and many related issues were pathbreaking applications of economics to law that continue to influence economists, legal scholars, and policymakers even many decades later.

In addition to his many contributions to law and economics, Posner also published enormously influential books and articles on a dizzying array of other issues. I can only mention a few here. His book Sex and Reason is a tremendously insightful analysis of legal regulation of intimate relationships. How Judges Think and Reflections on Judging shed light on a variety of issues relating to judicial behavior, and legal philosophy. Law and Literature is one of the greatest books on the depiction of law in classic literary works. This list of pathbreaking Posner works can be extended almost endlessly!

Posner became a federal appellate judge in 1981 (appointed to the US Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit). There, he became perhaps the most influential federal lower court judge of his time, writing a variety of widely cited opinions. He was famous in legal circles for drafting almost all of his opinions himself, rarely relying on law clerks to do it.

A few of my own experiences with Posner and his work may shed some small additional light on the man and his achievements.

As a first-year law student, I was required to take an early-morning Contracts class. Not being a morning person, I periodically overslept and missed class (Posner, I'm sure, would never have done such a thing!). As a result, I was confused about some issues when final exam time came around. The class textbook was only of limited help in clearing up my confusion. So I decided to read the contracts chapter of Economic Analysis of Law. In a relatively few pages, Posner made everything much clearer, and I came to a much better understanding of a wide range of contracts issues than I had before, from studying the much longer textbook. Thanks to Posner, I did much better on the exam than I had any right to expect. He had a gift for distilling complex issues of law and public policy and making them readily understandable even to late-sleeping slackers!

A few years later, I was a law clerk for a federal appellate judge. Usually, when courts cite legal precedents, they do not indicate the name of the judge who wrote the decision. But my judge - who is more conservative than Posner and has a very different judicial philosophy - made clear that, when citing a Posner opinion, I should make sure to indicate Posner was the author. It's a small, but telling, indication of the respect Posner commanded from jurists across the political and jurisprudential spectrum.

Early in my academic career, I was co-editor of the Supreme Court Economic Review. One of the more difficult duties of academic journal editors is dealing with peer reviewers, who often procrastinate,  submit inadequate reviews, or both. One time, on a Friday afternoon, I e-mailed Posner an article submission, asking him to review it. Due to his simultaneous work as legal scholar and judge, Posner was almost certainly much busier than most of our other reviewers. Still, on Saturday morning, I woke up to find a message from Posner in my e-mail inbox. I expected the message would indicate whether he accepted the assignment or not. But instead, I found an extremely thorough and insightful review of the article I had sent him - one of the best peer review reports I have ever seen. In addition to his many other achievements and talents, Posner was extraordinarily hard-working and efficient. He made most of the rest of us seem lazy and indolent by comparison.

I was privileged to know Posner over a period of many years, though we interacted only occasionally. Most of my professional writings related to his work were critical, as in the case of my review of his book Law, Pragmatism, and Democracy, (to which he wrote a solid response,  and I in turn did a short rejoinder), and my criticism (in my book The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain) of his defense of the Supreme Court's controversial ruling in Kelo v. City of New London.

In retrospect, I fear these writings did not always sufficiently convey the enormous respect - even awe - that I had for Posner's many achievements. But I did support his longstanding campaign to get rid of the Bluebook, the ridiculously overcomplicated system of legal citation. In general, I am not a fan of book-burning. But I was happy to follow Posner in making an exception for the Bluebook! For a time, we even collaborated on an effort to persuade law journal editors to rethink the system.

Much, much more can be said. No words of mine can even come close to doing justice to Judge Posner's many achievements, or to his generosity to students and younger colleagues, of which my own experiences with him were just small examples. Thus, I will close by offering my profound condolences to those of his friends, family, and colleagues, who might read this post.

UPDATE: For more on Judge Posner's life and achievements, see this obituary on the University of Chicago Law School website.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.
